m1_f16sa_4.stem: (3 points) These questions will ask about how the Scientific Method is used to evaluate and develop models of the economy. A. Why do economists look at correlations between pieces of economic data? Explain why they are useful statistics. B. How do economists use economic models to get model predictions that can be compared to the correlations in the data? C. Explain why “shocks” to the demand side of our one-period model (preferences or Government) are never going to explain all the key business cycle statistics we’ve seen in class.
m1_f16sa_4.officialRubric:
(3 points) These questions will ask about how the Scientific Method is used to evaluate and develop models of the economy.
Why do economists look at correlations between pieces of economic data? Explain why they are useful statistics.
1 point: There are common relationships between variables that exist across all business cycles, even though plausibly each of the many cycles may have been caused for different reasons. Those correlations are therefore stable and our models should be able to replicate them no matter what is going on.
How do economists use economic models to get model predictions that can be compared to the correlations in the data?
1 point: We can’t get ‘correlations’ between equations because equations don’t move. But we can look at first derivatives to see how endogenous variables defined at the equilibrium respond to changes in exogenous variables to see if the size of correlations is roughly the same as in the data.
Explain why “shocks” to the demand side of our one-period model (preferences or Government) are never going to explain all the key business cycle statistics we’ve seen in class.
1 point: Real wages are procyclical in the data. The only way for the real wage to rise as GDP rises in the model is if productivity has increased, and so the only way to get real wages to be procyclical is from a productivity shock, not a preference change or change in Government/taxes.

m1_s17sa_7.officialRubric:
(2 points) The Solow Residual
What is the Solow Residual and how is it measured?
1⁄2 point: It is a measure of technology
1⁄2 point: It is measured as the residual of output and the contributions of K and L to GDP
Explain one reason that measurement error in the Solow Residual may make our one-period model from class look like a better explanation of business cycles than it actually is.
1 point Movements in the Solow Residual look like movements in GDP, which is what the model says, but those movements in the Solow residual may really be caused by a missing input in the production function that isn’t being measured separately and is instead lumped in with productivity in the Solow Residual. Thus the thing that works best in the model-productivity—might not matter much in the real world

m1_s17sa_8.stem: (3 points) What three properties do the preferences of the representative consumer have? Explain the importance of each to our one-period model.
m1_s17sa_8.officialRubric:
(3 points) What three properties do the preferences of the representative consumer have? Explain the importance of each to our one-period model.
1 point: Utility is increasing in both consumption and leisure. This assumption gives us a substitution effect between the two (as leisure foregone earns income to buy consumption goods)—or can say an opportunity cost or tradeoff or points of indifference.
1 point: Consumer prefer more to less (or can say both Consumption and leisure are normal goods). As incomes rise, households prefer more of the goods in their utility functions—they are normal. That also means that we can rank utility so that as income rises we are on a higher indifference curve. (Any of these arguments are valid)
1 point: Consumers prefer diversity. That causes our indifference curves to be convex, which means that high degrees of specialization in either C or leisure must be the result of extremes in slope of the budget constraint.
